subject: physics

moments.title: Slipher measures galaxy redshifts
moments.body:
Slipher (working alone, with old equipment) takes spectra of 'spiral nebulae' (now known to be other galaxies). Most are redshifted, suggesting they are moving away. By 1917 he has measurements for 25 of them.

What the spirals are — clouds in our galaxy, or distant 'island universes' — is still disputed.
moments.takeaway: The data are there, but the interpretation depends on knowing what spiral nebulae are.

moments.title: Hubble proves Andromeda is its own galaxy
moments.body:
Using the 100-inch Hooker Telescope (then the largest in the world), Hubble identifies Cepheid variable stars in the Andromeda nebula. Their period-luminosity relation (calibrated by Henrietta Leavitt in 1912) gives the distance: about 1 million light-years (we now know it's 2.5 million).

Andromeda is far outside the Milky Way. The universe is much bigger than anyone had supposed.
moments.takeaway: The Milky Way is not the universe. It's one of many galaxies.

moments.title: Lemaître proposes expansion from a singular point
moments.body:
Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist, applies Einstein's field equations and proposes the universe is expanding from an initial 'primeval atom'. He derives a velocity-distance relation: v = H * d, two years before Hubble's empirical version.

Lemaître's paper is in French and in a small Belgian journal. Einstein dismisses the idea: 'Your calculations are correct, but your physics is abominable.'
moments.takeaway: The Big Bang was proposed before Hubble's data forced the issue. Einstein resists for years.

moments.title: Hubble's law
moments.body:
Hubble publishes recession velocities (from Slipher's data) vs distances (his own measurements) for 24 galaxies. The relation is linear: v = H * d. Distance galaxies recede faster.

This is the canonical evidence for an expanding universe. Hubble himself was cautious about the interpretation — he sometimes preferred to say galaxies SEEM to recede.
moments.takeaway: The universe is expanding. The further away you look, the faster it's receding.

moments.title: Penzias and Wilson discover the cosmic microwave background
moments.who: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, Bell Labs, Holmdel
moments.body:
Penzias and Wilson are calibrating a horn antenna for radio astronomy. They detect a uniform 'noise' from all directions at about 3 Kelvin. They scrub the antenna for pigeon droppings — still there.

A nearby Princeton group (Dicke, Peebles, Roll, Wilkinson) had predicted exactly this: cooled-down photons from a hot Big Bang. The two groups publish back to back. Penzias and Wilson win the 1978 Nobel Prize.
moments.takeaway: The Big Bang's afterglow is detected by accident. Cosmology becomes a precision science.

now.title: Cosmology today
now.body:
The universe is 13.787 billion years old (Planck satellite, 2018). It contains about 5 percent ordinary matter, 27 percent dark matter and 68 percent dark energy. The Cosmic Microwave Background is the most precisely measured electromagnetic spectrum in physics, agreeing with a blackbody at 2.7255 K to better than 1 part in 10,000.

JWST (launched 2021) is now imaging galaxies less than 300 million years after the Big Bang.
now.open_questions: What's dark matter? What's dark energy? Why is the universe so smooth at large scales (the horizon problem)? Inflation gives an explanation but raises new questions. What came before the Big Bang? Did the universe have a beginning, or has it always been? Are there multiple universes?

reflection: Lemaître proposed the expanding universe in 1927 — two years before Hubble's data — and proposed the Big Bang in 1931. Yet 'Hubble's law' bears Hubble's name, not Lemaître's. In 2018 the International Astronomical Union officially renamed it the Hubble-Lemaître law. How long does science wait to correct attribution, and what does the delay tell us about how we remember discovery?
